question: Why do trained ReLU Transformer MLPs activate so few neurons per input, and can that dynamic activation sparsity improve computation, robustness, and calibration?

key_findings.claim: ReLU activation maps become far sparser during Transformer training than their approximately 50% nonzero rate at random initialization.
key_findings.evidence: A T5-Base span-corruption run ends at about 2.7% nonzeros averaged across encoder and decoder MLPs, with individual layers between roughly 1.1% and 12%; ViT-B/16 also reaches a low single-digit average rate.

key_findings.claim: The effect appears across model families, layers, data splits, and training configurations, and wider or deeper networks tend to use a smaller percentage but not necessarily a smaller count of neurons.
key_findings.evidence: The main experiments cover T5 and ViT on language and vision, while appendices add BERT, MLP-Mixer, ResNets, and two-layer MLPs. Controlled T5 sweeps show lower activation fractions with depth and width, but wider MLPs still activate more neurons in absolute count.

key_findings.claim: Dynamic sparsity does not mean that most MLP neurons are globally dead or removable.
key_findings.evidence: Across about 409,600 token activations in one T5 layer, roughly 93.5% of neurons fire on fewer than 10% of inputs, yet no neuron is entirely dead and about 99% fire on more than 1% of inputs; different tokens select different long-tail subsets.

key_findings.claim: Meaningful labels, natural input structure, and finite-data interpolation each affect sparsity but are not necessary for activation rates to fall below initialization.
key_findings.evidence: ViTs trained with random labels, random pixels, or a stream of never-repeated random image-label pairs remain substantially below 50% nonzeros, although layerwise rates shift and some infinite-data middle layers rise toward 10-20%.

key_findings.claim: Theorem 3.1 gives a narrow initialization-time mechanism: for a random independent zero-mean last layer, expected MSE or cross-entropy gradient descent reduces each positive penultimate preactivation.
key_findings.evidence: The theorem covers a generic network ending in ReLU and a random linear readout. Its proof shows a positive expected loss derivative with respect to a positive preactivation under stated independence assumptions.

key_findings.claim: A hard Top-k MLP can preserve the studied T5 and ViT task accuracy at moderate k and gives a modest demonstrated latency reduction in one decode regime.
key_findings.evidence: T5-3B with k=128 and ViT with k=256 are within about 0.3 percentage points of dense counterparts. A custom second-layer path reduces unbatched greedy-decoding latency on one TPUv4 by roughly 10% for T5-11B at k at most 128.

key_findings.claim: Top-k and activation-norm regularization improve the paper's selected noise-robustness and calibration metrics at similar clean accuracy.
key_findings.evidence: On ImageNet-1k, Top-128 ViT holds clean top-1 near 74.8%, improves results under 40% and 80% label noise and three ImageNet-C noise types, and reduces ECE from 8.42% to 7.48%; L1 and L2 activation penalties reproduce parts of the trend.

key_findings.claim: The experiments do not establish that training dynamics alone cause useful sparsity or that sparsity itself causes robustness.
key_findings.evidence: The theorem applies only at random-readout initialization and not later training, the infinite random-label task remains at chance and can reduce activations without learning structure, and Top-k changes effective capacity and regularization along with sparsity without matched alternative-capacity controls.

key_findings.claim: The phrase efficiency for free overstates what native ReLU sparsity directly supplies on dense accelerators.
key_findings.evidence: Exact zeros immediately skip only the second MLP projection if a sparse kernel is efficient; accelerating the first projection requires an unimplemented approximate maximum-inner-product search, and the paper explicitly says current hardware poorly supports the data-dependent pattern.

method.core_idea: Measure per-token ReLU MLP activation rates across trained Transformers, stress competing causal explanations, and impose Top-k activity to test whether the emergent pattern is useful.
method.mechanism: The observational study records exact post-ReLU zeros by layer and neuron over language and vision data, then varies architecture, labels, inputs, data reuse, optimizer, and residual structure. A generic initialization theorem analyzes gradient sign, while a Top-k operator or activation penalty explicitly controls active neurons for efficiency and regularization experiments.
assumptions: Exact ReLU zeros are a meaningful definition of activation sparsity and transfer to architectures using smooth gated activations.
Random-label and random-input interventions isolate candidate causes without introducing degenerate optimization behavior.
Initialization-time expected gradients remain informative about sparsity over extended training.
Top-k gating is an adequate intervention for testing the consequences of naturally emergent sparsity.
FLOP reductions can be realized by sparse search and kernels without losing the dense model's quality.
Selected corruption accuracy and ECE reflect a broad reliability benefit.

techniques.role: Measures token-wise nonzero rates and per-neuron firing-frequency distributions.
Separates effects of depth, width, model family, residual structure, and optimizer.
Tests whether semantic labels, natural inputs, or finite-data fitting are necessary for sparsity.
Shows an expected pressure toward smaller positive activations under a random readout.
Guarantees a fixed activation budget during training and inference.
Checks whether L1- or L2-induced low activity reproduces reliability trends.
Demonstrates limited wall-clock benefit from skipping zero-weighted columns during decoding.

evaluations.setting: T5 and ViT pretraining across model sizes, layers, training/evaluation splits, and data scales.
evaluations.metric: Percentage and count of nonzero post-ReLU MLP activations.
evaluations.result: Low single-digit activation fractions are common; larger models usually have lower fractions, although wider models activate more neurons in absolute count.
evaluations.baseline: Approximately 50% nonzeros at random initialization and smaller architecture configurations.

evaluations.setting: BERT, MLP-Mixer, ResNet, and two-layer MLP appendix studies with optimizer and residual variants.
evaluations.metric: Layerwise activation rate and training accuracy.
evaluations.result: Sparsity extends beyond Transformers but varies strongly by layer type, normalization, activation function, optimizer, learning rate, and parameterization regime.
evaluations.baseline: T5/ViT patterns and alternative architecture/training variants.

evaluations.setting: ViT with corrupted labels, random images, or an effectively infinite stream of random image-label pairs.
evaluations.result: All conditions end below initialization density, but the layer profiles differ and the infinite random task does not learn beyond chance.

evaluations.setting: Top-k T5 up to 11B and ViT training, plus unbatched TPUv4 greedy decoding.
evaluations.result: Moderate k nearly matches dense task accuracy; the largest T5 shows about a 10% latency reduction in the specialized decode experiment.

evaluations.setting: ImageNet-1k with label corruption, ImageNet-C additive noise, and prediction calibration.
evaluations.metric: Clean/noisy top-1 accuracy and expected calibration error.
evaluations.result: Top-128 and suitably weighted activation penalties improve the tested corruption and calibration numbers with little clean-accuracy loss.
evaluations.baseline: Vanilla ViT under the same training setup.

limitations: Headline sparsity is exact only for ReLU; GELU and sigmoid evidence is a negative preactivation shift, not a high rate of exact zero outputs, and modern SwiGLU models differ further.
Theorem 3.1 concerns a generic final ReLU/readout at initialization and does not explain layerwise Transformer sparsity after features and labels become dependent on weights.
Random-label and infinite-data experiments rule out simple necessities but do not identify a sufficient causal mechanism.
Top-k sparsity, reduced effective capacity, altered gradient routing, and regularization are not independently controlled in the robustness study.
Only a narrow set of corruptions and calibration metrics is tested; adversarial, distribution-shift, sequence-generation, and rare-feature reliability are not established.
Dynamic activation sparsity cannot directly prune globally inactive parameters because almost every neuron fires somewhere.
The first MLP projection remains dense in the demonstrated system; approximate neighbor search is proposed but not evaluated for quality or runtime.
Wall-clock evidence is one unbatched TPUv4 decode workload and reaches about 10%, far below the nominal second-projection FLOP reduction.
failure_modes: Rare tokens may require neurons that look globally cold, making static pruning or cache placement brittle.
Hard Top-k selection can suppress multiple moderately useful features when a token needs distributed evidence.
Approximate active-neuron prediction can introduce compounding autoregressive errors despite high average recall.
Sparse indexing, sorting, and irregular memory access can cost more than dense matrix multiplication.
ReLU replacement can create dead regions or degrade smooth gated computations in modern LLMs.
Activation collapse on unlearnable random targets can look parsimonious while conveying no useful representation.
Robustness gains at one k can reverse when sparsity becomes too aggressive, as the regularization appendix indicates.
reusable_insights: Report both active fraction and active count; width can lower the first while increasing the second.
Distinguish dynamic per-input sparsity from structural sparsity and globally dead neurons.
Measure exact zeros, near-zero magnitudes, and predictable contextual sparsity separately for smooth activations.
A useful sparse architecture needs co-design across selection, first projection, second projection, memory layout, and accelerator kernels.
Causal claims about sparsity require matched capacity and regularization controls, not only Top-k versus dense comparisons.
Treat failed-task activation collapse as a negative control rather than evidence of efficient representation.
open_questions: What training-time mechanism sustains negative preactivation bias after the random-readout assumptions cease to hold?
How do activation rates and neuron reuse scale in modern SwiGLU LLMs trained for trillions of tokens?
Can active neurons be predicted cheaply enough to skip both MLP projections without sequence-quality loss?
Which reliability benefits survive matched bottleneck, dropout, weight decay, and compute controls?
How stable are rare-neuron routes across domains, languages, context lengths, fine-tuning, and quantization?
What accelerator primitives make token-dependent unstructured sparsity faster across both prefill and decoding?

competitive_landscape.title: ReLU Strikes Back: Exploiting Activation Sparsity in Large Language Models
competitive_landscape.difference: ReLU Strikes Back studies replacing modern LLM activations with ReLU, neuron reuse across decoding tokens, and practical inference strategies with larger speedups; the target establishes the broader emergence phenomenon and Top-k proof of concept on T5/ViT.

competitive_landscape.title: Deja Vu: Contextual Sparsity for Efficient LLMs at Inference Time
competitive_landscape.difference: DejaVu predicts input-dependent sparse attention heads and MLP parameters and reports end-to-end OPT-175B latency gains with asynchronous hardware-aware execution; the target mostly counts native zeros and accelerates only the second MLP projection in one workload.

competitive_landscape.title: ProSparse: Introducing and Enhancing Intrinsic Activation Sparsity within Large Language Models
competitive_landscape.difference: ProSparse replaces Swish with ReLU and gradually raises an activation-sparsity penalty during continued training to reach roughly 88-89% zeros in LLaMA2-scale models; the target uses natural ReLU sparsity, fixed Top-k, and smaller pretraining recipes.

competitive_landscape.title: Training-Free Activation Sparsity in Large Language Models
competitive_landscape.difference: TEAL prunes activations by magnitude without retraining and demonstrates sparse kernels on Llama-2, Llama-3, and Mistral up to 70B; it does not require exact ReLU zeros but introduces approximation error absent from native zero skipping.

competitive_landscape.title: Learning Neural Networks with Sparse Activations
competitive_landscape.difference: Awasthi et al. formalize learning under dynamic activation sparsity and the difficulty of exploiting it efficiently; the target's theorem supplies only an initialization gradient sign and does not give end-to-end sparse-learning guarantees.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: Extreme activation sparsity emerges ubiquitously in trained Transformers, likely from training dynamics, and can make models more efficient, robust, and calibrated through simple Top-k gating.
novelty_assessment.evidence: Large observational sweeps, random-data interventions, an initialization theorem, Top-k accuracy and latency tests, and corruption/calibration experiments support different parts of the claim.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The cross-architecture measurement study made dynamic MLP sparsity a concrete research target and the long-tail neuron analysis is especially reusable. Causation and free efficiency are less established: the proof is initialization-only, useful sparsity is entangled with regularization, and realized speed requires predictors and hardware support developed more fully by successors.

reviewer_notes: Read all 35 extracted pages, including random-data interventions, Theorem 3.1 and proof, architecture/optimizer/finetuning appendices, L1/L2 controls, two-layer MLP phase behavior, and FAQ. Exact ReLU sparsity is kept distinct from negative GELU preactivations, and nominal FLOPs are kept distinct from the roughly 10% demonstrated latency gain. Current arXiv and PMLR successors were checked on 2026-08-23.
